subject: science
passage: James Hutton proposed in 1788 that the Earth's landscapes had been shaped by the same slow processes of erosion and uplift observable in the present, acting over a span of time too vast to measure. His prose, however, was so dense that few readers got through it. A generation later, Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology, issued in three volumes between 1830 and 1833, set out the same principle with an abundance of examples in plain, persuasive English. ______ when Charles Darwin sailed on the Beagle in 1831, it was the first volume of Lyell, not Hutton, that he carried with him, and it was through Lyell that Hutton's time scale became the silent premise of the Origin of Species.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

explanation.why: The second and third sentences contrast Hutton's unreadable prose with Lyell's clear and persuasive presentation of the same idea. The last sentence reports the consequence: it was Lyell's book that reached Darwin and shaped his work. A transition marking that consequence is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Darwin's choice of Lyell's book does not stand in spite of Lyell's clarity; it is explained by it.
explanation.B: Correct. "Thus" shows that, because Lyell presented the idea clearly where Hutton had not, it was Lyell's book that Darwin read and relied on.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The last sentence is not a parallel case to Lyell's publication; it is what followed from it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The last sentence does not restate the description of Lyell's book; it describes its effect on Darwin.
